D-Wave Partners with University of Arkansas to Establish Quantum Supply Chain Initiative At the Sam M. Walton College of Business
D-WAVE QUANTUM INC.
D-Wave Quantum Inc. and the Supply Chain Management Research Center in the Sam M. Walton College of Business at the University of Arkansas (SCMRC) announced a collaboration to explore quantum computing?s impact on complex supply chain problems. The collaboration establishes the Quantum Supply Chain Initiative Support Fund with the SCMRC, which is intended to advance thought leadership, education and independent research focused on the application of quantum computing to supply chain management across retail, transportation and national defense. In addition, D-Wave has joined the partnership program of the SCMRC, which currently has more than 25 industry partners. Supply chain decision-making often requires organizations to coordinate routes, inventory, facilities, schedules and workforce while balancing cost, speed, service and resilience.
As these networks become more complex and disruptions become more consequential, quantum and hybrid-quantum computing approaches are emerging to complement established methods. Announced during CSCMP EDGE 2026, a leading conference and exhibition hosted by the Council of Supply Chain Management Professionals, the collaboration between D-Wave and the SCMRC will explore foundational and applied research in quantum optimization for a variety of supply chain use cases, including transportation routing, logistics network design, inventory and resource allocation, scheduling and decision-making under disruption. In addition, joint efforts may include curriculum and case development, student learning opportunities, engagement with industry, government and academic stakeholders and the development and sharing of practical frameworks and insights.

LOS ANGELES, CA - October 5, 2026 (NEWMEDIAWIRE) - D-Wave Quantum Inc. (NASDAQ: QBTS) ("D-Wave" or the "Company"), the only dual-platform quantum computing company providing both annealing and gate-model systems, software and services, recently launched its gate-model quantum computing simulator beta program, marking an important milestone in D-Wave's gate-model development roadmap.
The beta program offers select customers early access to the simulator in advance of its general availability to experiment with error-aware programming and develop quantum applications in preparation for D-Wave's forthcoming gate-model systems. The simulator is built around D-Wave's dual-rail superconducting gate-model technology, which is designed to harness error detection to deliver efficient quantum error correction with significantly lower hardware overhead as systems scale. Participants in the simulator beta program include commercial and research organizations: BBVA, FirstQFM, Florida Atlantic University (FAU) and the Julich Supercomputing Centre (JSC).

Quantum computing has gained increasing attention in recent years. Amid the technology's potential for exponentially faster computing, companies like Alphabet, IBM, and Nvidia have taken an interest in it.
Additionally, many smaller, pure-play quantum computing stocks have emerged, and two of the more prominent ones are IonQ (IONQ -1.83%) and D-Wave Quantum (QBTS -0.82%).
Although these stocks carry significant risks, their smaller sizes also offer greater potential for higher returns should they succeed. Thus, it is worth asking which of these stocks might be the better stock to buy.
Image source: The Motley Fool.
One limitation of quantum computing is that the technology is often error-prone. This means any company that can minimize that problem has a better chance of success, and IonQ may have the solution with its trapped-ion quantum system.
Last year, IonQ demonstrated 2-qubit gate fidelities of 99.99%. This technology unlocked more complex applications that could now be performed with minimal error rates. While that does not make it faster than its big-tech counterparts, it performs tasks with industry-leading precision.
Furthermore, the company, often called the "Nvidia of quantum," has formed a partnership with that company. Under the terms of the agreement, Nvidia will install the IonQ Superion 256 system at the Nvidia Accelerated Quantum Research Center. This will tie IonQ into Nvidia's ecosystem, which could give it a competitive advantage.
Unfortunately, such gains may not yet provide sufficient support for its financials. Its $145 million in revenue in the first half of 2026 was well above the $28 million in the same period a year ago, indicating it is growing faster than Nvidia. However, high operating expenses led to a $1.06 billion operating loss in the first two quarters of 2026, well above the $210 million loss from the same time frame last year.

Moreover, IonQ stock is down by more than one-third over the last year. Despite that decline, it still has a price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of around 65, an indication that the company's fundamentals have little bearing on the stock price. Such a valuation makes it extremely difficult to forecast IonQ's near-term direction at this time.
Why investors might consider D-Wave Quantum
Nonetheless, investors might also find challenges amid the potential in D-Wave Quantum. In an industry where some have predicted commercial viability is years away, Leap's quantum cloud service already runs customer applications.
Additionally, it has become a leader in optimization, as its quantum annealing technology helps find solutions while analyzing millions of variables. For example, AT&T cut a one-hour task down to less than 15 seconds using this application.
Thus, it is likely not surprising that companies use its technology to retrain AI models, generate molecular structures, and lower energy consumption.
However, much like with IonQ, D-Wave Quantum is far from profitability. In the first half of 2026, revenue of $5.9 million fell 67% year over year, though a large system sale in early 2025 skewed these results. Also, high operating expenses led to a $66 million loss for the same period.

Amid that financial performance, the stock dropped by almost 40% over the last year. Furthermore, at a P/S ratio of approximately 475, the stock's valuation factors in several years of anticipated revenue gains, making the stock a risky buy at this time.
Should investors buy IonQ or D-Wave Quantum?
As conditions stand now, both stocks face deep uncertainty in the foreseeable future, and risk-averse investors should probably avoid both of them. Nonetheless, if choosing one, I recommend IonQ.
Although D-Wave's success at applying the technology now is noteworthy, one cannot deny IonQ's built-in credibility that comes with its Nvidia partnership.
Moreover, while both are too expensive, it is less risky to pay around 65 times sales than it is to buy at a P/S ratio of around 475. Thus, amid significant uncertainty, IonQ looks like the safer buy that offers a higher probability of success.

D-Wave Quantum is widening its push into logistics and defense research while preparing to host its flagship user conference in Asia next year, a twin offensive that lands as investors grow impatient for proof that quantum computing can generate recurring commercial revenue.
The Canadian quantum specialist used the CSCMP EDGE 2026 industry gathering to unveil a collaboration with the Supply Chain Management Research Center at the University of Arkansas. The partnership establishes a Quantum Supply Chain Initiative Support Fund, which will bankroll independent research, teaching programs and case studies across three priority fields: retail, transportation and national defense. Researchers intend to examine whether quantum algorithms can outpace classical methods in vehicle routing, logistics network control, inventory management and the allocation of scarce resources. A particular focus will fall on decision-making during acute supply disruptions.
Under the arrangement, D-Wave joins a partner program that already counts more than 25 industrial participants, giving the company a direct line to potential adopters in business and government. The move builds on a partnership announced roughly two weeks earlier with CGI Global covering transport and commerce solutions, and it sits alongside an agreement with the US Department of Commerce worth up to USD 100 million in funding through the CHIPS Act.
Wall Street Wants Receipts, Not Roadmaps
Market reaction to the Arkansas announcement was muted. D-Wave shares (NASDAQ: QBTS) slipped 1.2 percent to EUR 13.85 in the session, extending a bruising run that has wiped 39 percent off the stock since the start of the year. In German trading the equity was quoted at EUR 14.20, well below its 200-day moving average of EUR 17.91 — a gap that underscores the downward pressure the shares have faced for months.
The sector-wide retreat came to a head last Friday, when quantum stocks came under heavy selling pressure amid industry-wide questions about valuations and persistent uncertainty over how quickly commercial adoption will arrive. For D-Wave, that headwind is arriving at an awkward moment, just as the company works to broaden its technological reach.
Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying D-Wave Quantum?
At the heart of the debate is a single question: when will technological partnerships translate into durable, growing revenue? Quantum computing spent years as a pure future bet with very long development cycles. Investors now demand tangible evidence of value in day-to-day industrial operations. Tie-ups with IT service providers demonstrate that established corporations are paying attention, but the decisive test is whether customers will commit to recurring software and cloud spending. Should that transition stall, the strain between heavy research budgets and hesitant bookings could erode investor confidence for good.
Not everyone sees near-term upside in optimization. Helmut Katzgraber of investment firm 55North recently argued that classical computing systems are likely to retain the upper hand in optimization tasks for the foreseeable future, pointing instead to materials and chemistry simulation as the more promising near-term opportunity for quantum machines.
Supporters point to D-Wave's steady opening of its product suite to new user groups. The company launched a gate-model simulator that grants selected organizations from industry and academia early access to tools for fault-tolerant programming. Participants include BBVA, FirstQFM, Florida Atlantic University and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre, with delivery running through the company's Leap cloud service and its Ocean SDK developer kit. The beta program, which began on a Thursday, lets testers work with applications built on Dual-Rail technology designed to detect errors at the hardware level.
The company also strengthened its leadership bench in technology and security. Bernard Gavgani, a technology and innovation adviser to the Group Executive Management of BNP Paribas and formerly the bank's CIO, joined the Board of Directors and the cybersecurity committee. That kind of network could accelerate acceptance of quantum architectures in finance and the corporate world — and if these initiatives convert into rising orders soon, a meaningful re-rating could follow.
The bear case rests on institutional caution that shows no sign of lifting. Friday's selloff illustrated how sensitive the entire sector is to doubts about profitability; without fresh corporate deals, the downtrend in the share chart could harden. A key risk lies in the length of customer onboarding: many industrial firms are still testing quantum approaches in pilot projects without releasing long-term budgets. If the broader market climate for unprofitable growth companies tightens, capital could become scarce.

Collaboration will facilitate education and research into quantum computing applications for supply chain challenges in retail, transportation and national defense
PALO ALTO, Calif. & FAYETTEVILLE, Ark., October 05, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--D-Wave Quantum Inc. (NASDAQ: QBTS) ("D-Wave"), the only dual-platform quantum computing company providing annealing and gate-model systems, software and services, and the Supply Chain Management Research Center in the Sam M. Walton College of Business at the University of Arkansas (SCMRC) today announced a collaboration to explore quantum computing's impact on complex supply chain problems. The collaboration establishes the Quantum Supply Chain Initiative Support Fund with the SCMRC, which is intended to advance thought leadership, education and independent research focused on the application of quantum computing to supply chain management across retail, transportation and national defense. In addition, D-Wave has joined the partnership program of the SCMRC, which currently has more than 25 industry partners.
Supply chain decision-making often requires organizations to coordinate routes, inventory, facilities, schedules and workforce while balancing cost, speed, service and resilience. As these networks become more complex and disruptions become more consequential, quantum and hybrid-quantum computing approaches are emerging to complement established methods.
Announced during CSCMP EDGE 2026, a leading conference and exhibition hosted by the Council of Supply Chain Management Professionals, the collaboration between D-Wave and the SCMRC will explore foundational and applied research in quantum optimization for a variety of supply chain use cases, including transportation routing, logistics network design, inventory and resource allocation, scheduling and decision-making under disruption. In addition, joint efforts may include curriculum and case development, student learning opportunities, engagement with industry, government and academic stakeholders and the development and sharing of practical frameworks and insights.
"Supply chains are highly dynamic, with decision-making that can have a far-reaching impact on efficiency and costs," said Murray Thom, vice president of quantum technology evangelism at D-Wave. "We're seeing quantum computing technologies emerge as potentially powerful alternatives to existing classical approaches. The Walton College is at the forefront of supply chain innovation, not only educating the next generation of supply chain professionals and conducting groundbreaking research, but also engaging industry to effect economic change. We're thrilled to support the College as it facilitates a quantum-ready supply chain."
"The Walton College is dedicated to exploring the very latest methods, processes and technologies that advance supply chain management and resilience," said Brian Fugate, Associate Dean for Research and Graduate Programs with Walton College. "Quantum computing is showing great potential to help organizations accelerate decision-making, mitigate disruption and drive better operational outcomes. We're excited to partner with D-Wave, one of the quantum computing industry's foremost leaders, to bring quantum into our research portfolio and ultimately benefit students and partners alike."

For years, quantum computing lived in a comfortable limbo on global financial markets: revolutionary on paper, commercially distant in practice. University research grants, academic lab setups and glossy future promises shaped how the entire sector was perceived. D-Wave Quantum is now showing what it looks like when that early phase starts to fade — and the market is not entirely convinced by the view.
The clearest signal of this maturation sits in the company's governance. On September 21, D-Wave appointed Bernard Gavgani to its Board of Directors and Cybersecurity Committee. Gavgani serves as Senior Advisor for Technology and Innovation to the BNP Paribas Group Executive Management, bringing expertise in global technology strategy, AI governance, cybersecurity and operational transformation. His arrival follows the August 17 addition of Kevan P. Krysler, CFO of Carbon Robotics, to the Board of Directors and Audit Committee. Krysler carries broad leadership experience in finance and corporate governance at both listed and private technology companies.
Profiles like these are not assembled for the next academic conference. They point toward the demands of large institutional customers, strict security reviews and robust control structures — the unglamorous machinery of enterprise sales.
Evidence that this professionalization is translating into day-to-day business comes from Japan. Telecommunications group NTT DOCOMO launched its second production quantum application built on D-Wave systems on August 18. The results are concrete: the application cut location registration signals during daily peak load by 65.3% and reduced paging signals by 7.0%.
Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying D-Wave Quantum?
That is a measurable relief in live mobile networks rather than a theoretical benchmark under lab conditions. The company is also shoring up its technological base and market access. A funding agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce provides up to $100 million from the CHIPS and Science Act, directed at research and development of superconducting annealing and gate-model technologies. A strategic partnership with CGI adds the Advantage2 quantum computer and hybrid optimization tools to the service portfolio for corporate clients.
Despite these steps toward industrial anchoring, the trading floor remains cautious. The stock closed Friday at EUR 15.29, down 33% since the start of the year. That skepticism has a logic of its own: at a market capitalization equivalent to EUR 5.83 billion, little room exists for disappointment. Market participants want hard numbers, not feasibility demonstrations.
The hard numbers, so far, are thin. Analyst Craig Ellis of B. Riley Securities reaffirmed his buy rating on Monday and kept his price target at $40, with his confidence resting mainly on the medium-term potential of the computing architecture. S&P Global Market Intelligence noted that bookings could rise sharply this year — but also flagged that second-quarter revenue stalled at $3.1 million, flat year over year and short of expectations.
That gap is the core tension running through the stock. Growing bookings are a necessary precondition for future success, yet the exchange increasingly demands proof that those contracts convert reliably into actual revenue. Partnerships with established IT service providers such as CGI, aimed at unlocking concrete optimization projects in logistics and retail, are sensible moves to strengthen governance and open doors to large corporate customers. Still, every personnel or organizational realignment remains a promise about the future as long as the operating leverage fails to materialize.
The stock also sits a considerable distance from its 52-week high of EUR 40.41, a retreat that illustrates how quickly speculative goodwill evaporates when hard metrics lag behind hopes. D-Wave now faces the task of proving that operational efficiency gains in network operations can be converted into recurring, scalable revenue across the board. For investors, the decisive phase has begun: the era of pure future hope is giving way to an industrial trial by fire — one that favors those with a strong appetite for risk and plenty of patience.

That thesis deserves scrutiny. The enthusiasm surrounding quantum computing's technological promise has, for now, papered over a far less inspiring financial picture at the company itself.

Pioneering science earns respect. In public markets, though, what counts is the ability to convert technology into dependable revenue. As long as corporate customers treat quantum machines as test-bed experiments rather than production tools, the commercial foundation remains uncomfortably thin.
Spending Outpaces Growth by a Wide Margin
While sales stall, costs are surging. GAAP operating expenses jumped 93% year over year in the second quarter to $54.98 million, and the adjusted EBITDA loss widened to $37.1 million. The January completion of the Quantum Circuits acquisition is among the items weighing on the numbers.
Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying D-Wave Quantum?
The strain on the balance sheet is considerable. Free cash flow burned through $79 million in the first half of 2026, and cash plus marketable securities fell by $273.1 million over twelve months to $546.2 million. News that CFO John Markovich stepped down in early September — with Greg Golkov taking over on an interim basis — does little to inspire confidence in the company's financial stewardship.
Management's Hopes Rest on Year-End System Sales
D-Wave's leadership is now pointing to the fourth quarter. CEO Alan Baratz has flagged meaningful revenue growth ahead from the planned sale of two annealing systems.
Such deals, however, are lumpy one-off events rather than a substitute for recurring income. And the company does not expect fault-tolerant machines with 100 logical qubits until 2032 — a painfully long stretch for a technology that is already consuming substantial capital.
The shares changed hands at EUR 15.32 on the day of the primary report, down 32% since the start of the year and 62% below their 52-week high. No specific new funding commitments or company-level catalysts were cited as the trigger for the rating.
At current levels, the equity remains above all a speculative wager on the industrial adoption of quantum computers. The pivotal question is whether D-Wave can use the upcoming congress to demonstrate genuine commercial momentum and measurable market traction.
Until the company reins in its heavy cash outflows and proves it can generate predictable revenue, conference headlines and analyst endorsements offer little support for a lasting turnaround.

D-Wave Quantum closed Monday's session at EUR 15.44, a gain of 3.7% that rode a broad wave of enthusiasm across the quantum computing sector. The uptick offered a rare bright spot for a stock that has surrendered 32% since the start of the year — a decline that tells a more complicated story than any single trading day can.
At the heart of that story sits a widening gap between the company's technological ambitions and the commercial results it is currently delivering. For the first six months of 2026, D-Wave booked revenue of USD 5.9 million, down sharply from USD 18.1 million in the same period a year earlier — a 67% contraction. The second quarter alone brought in USD 3.08 million, falling short of the consensus estimates analysts had penciled in.
Those figures land with particular force given the company's valuation. D-Wave still trades at a very high price-to-sales multiple, and it carries a substantial net loss for fiscal 2025 alongside a low debt load. When a stock is priced for hypergrowth, any stumble in revenue expansion cuts deep. The market's patience is not infinite, and the recent numbers have tested it.
A Federal Commitment Worth Up to $100 Million
Against that commercial backdrop, Washington has stepped in with a meaningful vote of confidence. Roughly a week ago, the US Department of Commerce finalized a definitive agreement under the CHIPS and Science Act, granting D-Wave access to funding of up to USD 100 million. The money is earmarked for research and development, specifically to advance superconducting quantum systems spanning both annealing and gate-based models.
Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying D-Wave Quantum?
For a company burning capital through a hardware-intensive development phase, that commitment provides rare planning certainty. It cushions the heavy R&D burden and reinforces the technological foundation needed to compete globally. Yet subsidies are a catalyst, not a cure. They can accelerate the maturation of the hardware and lay groundwork for future commercial platforms, but they cannot by themselves manufacture durable market success.
A study published Monday in the journal Quantum Information Processing adds a note of caution from the laboratory side. Researchers examined noise models on the Advantage2 system, a processor built on the Zephyr architecture with up to 7,440 qubits. Their finding: as problem sizes grow, chain strength scaling behaves less favorably than earlier theoretical models had assumed.
In practical terms, embedding complex optimization tasks consumes more correction resources than customers might expect. The physical characteristics of the hardware impose real limits on how far commercial applications can stretch — a reminder that the distance between a working qubit count and a working business case is measured in more than just engineering milestones.
D-Wave is not waiting for the physics to sort itself out. Starting tomorrow, the company takes the floor at the Quantum World Congress 2026 in College Park, Maryland, running through September 25. The three-day event gives D-Wave a platform to present its systems, software, and specific applications to a technical audience.
A second date looms on October 28, 2026, when the company hosts Qubits Asia 2026 in Seoul — a full-day user conference designed to spotlight concrete customer deployments. Both events matter because investors increasingly want proof that quantum architectures can measurably speed up real workflows, not just theoretical benchmarks.
D-Wave Quantum at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now.
Alongside its public-facing push, D-Wave has adjusted its board. On Friday, the company appointed Bernard Gavgani as an independent Class II director, and he will also sit on the board's cybersecurity committee. The move signals how prominently data security and governance now figure as quantum systems edge closer to commercial networks.
Sell-side opinion remains, for now, constructive. The analyst consensus stands at "Moderate Buy" with an average price target of USD 36.27 — a level that implies substantial upside if the company can right the ship.
That "if" carries the weight of everything above. Euphoria phases in the quantum sector alternate regularly with sober reassessments, and Monday's gain shows how receptive the space remains to positive catalysts. But the overarching trend is a reminder that patience is the market's scarcest commodity. The decisive test for D-Wave is not a conference booth or a federal grant — it is whether quarterly revenue can return to growth. Until that happens, the stock will demand considerable risk tolerance from anyone who holds it.

Quantum computing has gained increasing attention in recent years. Amid the technology's potential for exponentially faster computing, companies like Alphabet, IBM, and Nvidia have taken an interest in it.
Additionally, many smaller, pure-play quantum computing stocks have emerged, and two of the more prominent ones are IonQ (IONQ -1.83%) and D-Wave Quantum (QBTS -0.82%).
Although these stocks carry significant risks, their smaller sizes also offer greater potential for higher returns should they succeed. Thus, it is worth asking which of these stocks might be the better stock to buy.

One limitation of quantum computing is that the technology is often error-prone. This means any company that can minimize that problem has a better chance of success, and IonQ may have the solution with its trapped-ion quantum system.
Last year, IonQ demonstrated 2-qubit gate fidelities of 99.99%. This technology unlocked more complex applications that could now be performed with minimal error rates. While that does not make it faster than its big-tech counterparts, it performs tasks with industry-leading precision.
Furthermore, the company, often called the "Nvidia of quantum," has formed a partnership with that company. Unfortunately, such gains may not yet provide sufficient support for its financials. Its $145 million in revenue in the first half of 2026 was well above the $28 million in the same period a year ago, indicating it is growing faster than Nvidia. Additionally, it has become a leader in optimization, as its quantum annealing technology helps find solutions while analyzing millions of variables. For example, AT&T cut a one-hour task down to less than 15 seconds using this application.

The bear case rests on institutional caution that shows no sign of lifting. A key risk lies in the length of customer onboarding: many industrial firms are still testing quantum approaches in pilot projects without releasing long-term budgets. If the broader market climate for unprofitable growth companies tightens, capital could become scarce.
The stock's path now hinges on concrete operational milestones. As long as the current annual low of EUR 11.12 holds, the broader recovery scenario for the quote remains intact; a sustained break below that mark under heavy selling would likely invite follow-on selling. Investors already have their next date circled: on October 28, 2026, D-Wave will host the Qubits Asia 2026 user conference in Seoul, where customers are expected to present real-world deployment reports and new research findings. Those presentations will reveal just how far practical industrial use has actually progressed.
